The boss explicitly asked for the path bar text to be selectable, so I'll add select-text to the FileCrumbs container in FileView.tsx. The empty-state detail showing missing file paths is technically chrome per the project rules, so I'll leave that alone and keep changes minimal.

Now I need to check where FileCrumbs is actually used and review the remaining files to see if there are other places that need the select-text treatment.

I'm understanding how the usage tracking works for assistant messages—each one emits a usage snapshot per content block with placeholder token counts, and then at the end of a turn the final usage with cost and a `total: true` flag replaces those intermediate values rather than adding to them. So during a turn the display shows those per-block usages, but they get consolidated at the end.

There's a couple of quirks though: the result line doesn't include a `model` field, so the model information is missing from the final usage object even though cost still comes through from `total_cost_usd`. And the result usage excludes tokens from Task subagent calls and haiku side-calls while the total cost includes them, which means tokens and cost can disagree on runs that use the Task tool. Also worth noting that crew pushes duplicate usage entries for the same message ID, which could double-count if the app sums them live, but since the final total replaces them anyway the end result is correct.

Checked the code path and had a helper probe the real CLI. Short answer: the price is right and the token count beside it is wrong, which is why the pair looks absurd.

**The $15.36 isn't crew's arithmetic.** Claude Code prices its own turn and puts `total_cost_usd` on the result line, and `claude.ts:122` passes that straight through. On a live probe that figure reconciled to the cent-fraction against Anthropic's published rates, cached prefixes and all. So it is a real number for the tokens the run moved.

**But it is a valuation, not a bill.** You're on a plan, so nobody charges you $15. It's what those tokens would have cost at API list price. That's what the note at the top of `pricing.ts` means when it says "the price of the tokens rather than a bill anyone is getting".

**The 7.2k is not the run's tokens.** It's output tokens only, and only from the main thread. `cli.ts:209` shows the count is `counted.output`. It leaves out every input token, the whole cached context re-read on each of the run's model calls, and, per the probe, everything a Task subagent spent and every Haiku side-call. Claude's result `usage` covers the top-level conversation and the main model, while `total_cost_usd` covers everything. On a run that fans out to subagents, the probe measured 314 output tokens sitting next to a price paid for 656 Opus plus 17 Haiku. So the two numbers on your row are measuring different work, and dividing one by the other tells you nothing.

For a 13-minute run, almost all of that $15 is context being re-read on every call plus whatever helpers it spawned. None of that is in the 7.2k.

Two things worth fixing, if you want them:

- The token count should read `modelUsage` off the result line instead of `usage`. That sums to the whole run, subagents included, and agrees with the cost. It also carries per-model attribution, which we can't get today because the result line has no `model` key at all, so `usage.model` is always undefined there.
- `CACHE_WRITE = 1.25` in `pricing.ts` is wrong for a 1-hour cached prefix, which bills at 2x base input. The two TTLs get mixed inside a single run, and the result line splits them under `cache_creation`. This only bites where crew prices a run itself rather than taking the CLI's figure, so it never touched your $15.36, but it under-reports everywhere it does apply.

One caveat: tokens and cost only ride in memory and the snapshot, never the event log, so I can't pull up that specific run to confirm its numbers. What I verified is the mechanism, on a fresh run.

Want me to fix the token count?

**But it is a valuation, not a bill.** You're on a plan, so nobody charges you $15. It's what those tokens would have cost at API list price. That's what the note at the top of `pricing.ts` means when it says "the price of the tokens rather than a bill anyone is getting".

**The 7.2k is not the run's tokens.** It's output tokens only, and only from the main thread. `cli.ts:209` shows the count is `counted.output`. It leaves out every input token, the whole cached context re-read on each of the run's model calls, and, per the probe, everything a Task subagent spent and every Haiku side-call. Claude's result `usage` covers the top-level conversation and the main model, while `total_cost_usd` covers everything. On a run that fans out to subagents, the probe measured 314 output tokens sitting next to a price paid for 656 Opus plus 17 Haiku. So the two numbers on your row are measuring different work, and dividing one by the other tells you nothing.

For a 13-minute run, almost all of that $15 is context being re-read on every call plus whatever helpers it spawned. None of that is in the 7.2k.

Two things worth fixing, if you want them:

- The token count should read `modelUsage` off the result line instead of `usage`. That sums to the whole run, subagents included, and agrees with the cost. It also carries per-model attribution, which we can't get today because the result line has no `model` key at all, so `usage.model` is always undefined there.
- `CACHE_WRITE = 1.25` in `pricing.ts` is wrong for a 1-hour cached prefix, which bills at 2x base input. The two TTLs get mixed inside a single run, and the result line splits them under `cache_creation`. This only bites where crew prices a run itself rather than taking the CLI's figure, so it never touched your $15.36, but it under-reports everywhere it does apply.

One caveat: tokens and cost only ride in memory and the snapshot, never the event log, so I can't pull up that specific run to confirm its numbers. What I verified is the mechanism, on a fresh run.

Want me to fix the token count?

N1 works best—at 48 pixels the nib with its vent hole sits on a line extending off both edges, clearly reading as a pen on paper, and at 16 pixels it stays crisp with a clean wedge nib and solid bar that's wider than the nib itself, avoiding any trophy-like appearance. The other options fall short: N2 feels too heavy, N3's short line reads more like a pedestal, N5 loses distinctiveness without the vent, and N4 alone doesn't convey writing.

I'm verifying the final specs for N1—the nib spans 11.9 units with a vent dot, and the line extends 18.5 units across both edges. The nib tip and line are positioned so they nearly touch at 16 pixels, which reinforces that the nib is sitting on the line. The vent dot at radius 1.3 renders as a crisp 2-pixel blob at small sizes. Now I'll run the icon build to check how it looks alongside the rest of the set and verify all the path coordinates are correct. Looking at the 48px render more carefully, the nib bottom does seem to splay slightly, but I should verify the arc direction by checking the bounding box dimensions after writing the file — if the tip bulged upward instead of downward, the height would be noticeably different. Let me finalize the geometry numbers and commit the icon.

Now I'm verifying the measurements: the nib spans from x 8.4 to 15.6 with a 2.35 corner radius, the shoulders sit at those computed coordinates, and the tip reaches down to around y 19.6. The vent is a small filled circle, and there's a line at the bottom. Checking the overall bounding box against the live area constraints to make sure everything fits within the keyline limits.

The size calculation comes out to 18.2, which is under the 19.5 cap, so it passes. The shape is marked as square with a target of 17, putting it about 7% oversized, but since it's capped that doesn't trigger a flag. The line running edge to edge is what creates that visual weight in the design.

I'm considering pulling the line in slightly to make the audit cleaner. If I adjust it to 17.5 wide, the size drops to 17.7 (4.1% over), which stays under the 8% tolerance without needing the cap excuse. Or splitting the difference at 18 wide gives 17.95 (5.6% over), still comfortably within tolerance and avoiding the cap flag entirely while keeping the line visually prominent relative to the nib.

Let me finalize with the line running from x 3 to x 21 at y 20.9, using NIB12 for the nib itself, and verify the mark count: outline, vent, and line equals three marks, which fits the "two or three marks" requirement. I'll name this ScribeGlyph and save it to media.t.

For placement, ScribeGlyph goes in media.tsx right after MicOffGlyph since the barrel already re-exports everything with `export *`. The file is the right location per the task requirements. I'm considering whether to add a comment — the file already has documentation explaining the drawing decisions, and the skill guidelines treat icon files as documented, so I should follow that pattern. I'll match the file's style and include a brief comment since every other glyph here has one—these notes are the design record for shapes that can't be understood from numbers alone. Now I'm finalizing the path strings, rounding to quarter units where the skill allows.

Adjusting the coordinates to cleaner values—shifting to 8.5 and 15.5 for the width at the top, rounding the corner radius to 2.25, and rebuilding the arc path cleanly so the shoulders flow properly from the top corners down through the angled sides.

Now I'm working out the geometry of the corner turn more precisely. The top edge runs horizontally while the flank angles downward and inward toward the tip, so I need to calculate the exact unit vectors for both directions to ensure the rounded corner transitions smoothly between them.

The interior angle at the corner works out to about 67.7°, which means for a fillet radius of 2.25, the tangent offset distance is roughly 3.35 units. This tells me where the arc should start and end relative to the actual vertex where those two edges would meet.

Now I need to find the exact vertex location where the top edge intersects with the flank line defined by the shoulder and tip positions.

I'm settling on a triangle with vertices at (6.1, 3), (17.9, 3), and (12, 19.6) — giving me an 11.8-unit-wide top edge. The rounded corners at radius 2.25 will cut into the top corners, and the apex gets a tighter 0.9-radius fillet. At the top-right corner (17.9, 3), the arc transitions from the horizontal top edge to the angled flank.

I'm calculating the arc geometry: the interior angle works out to about 70.4°, which gives me an offset distance of 3.19 units along each edge from the corner. So the arc starts at (14.71, 3) and ends at (16.83, 6.00).

Now I need to find where the arc actually reaches its maximum x-coordinate. The arc center sits at the intersection of the inward normals from both edges, which places it at (14.71, 5.25) with a radius of about 2.25 units. The rightmost point on the arc would be around x = 16.96, but I need to verify this point actually falls within the arc's endpoints.

The arc spans from 270° (straight up from the center) clockwise through 0° to about 19.5°, so it does pass through the rightmost point. That gives me a maximum width of 9.92 units, which is narrower than my target of 11.9. The rounded corners are consuming too much space, so I'll need to adjust the triangle's dimensions to compensate.

I'm recalculating with a wider triangle: the top edge now runs from (5.0, 3) to (19.0, 3) with the apex at (12, 19.6). Working through the right flank geometry—the direction vector, interior angle, and the arc parameters—I'm finding where the rounded corner reaches its maximum extent.

Now I'm moving to the apex arc with radius 0.9, computing the angle between the two flanks meeting at the peak and determining where the arc begins along each flank direction.

138·(0.3885,-0.9213) = (12.83, 17.63); ends at (11.17, 17.63). Centre = apex + (0, -r/sin(22.85°))= 19.6 - 0.9/0.3883 = 19.6 - 2.318 = 17.28 → centre (12, 17.28). Max y on the arc = 17.28 + 0.9 = 18.18.

Hmm, so with a 0.9 tip radius the actual bottom is 18.18, not 19.6. That's a much blunter tip than I want. To get the tip near 19.6 I should shrink the tip radius: r = 0.5 → centre y = 19.6 - 0.5/0.3883 = 19.6 - 1.288 = 18.31; bottom = 18.81. r = 0.35 → 19.6 - 0.901 = 18.70; bottom 19.05.

Actually, looking at how the pencil handles this—it uses a sharp vertex at the apex and relies on the stroke's round line join to create the visual roundness. I can do the same thing here: keep the apex sharp so the geometry measures exactly at 19.6, and let the stroke rendering handle the rounded appearance. This simplifies the path significantly.

So I'm going back to a sharp apex with rounded corners on the top edges via arcs.

Defining the nib path with rounded corners at radius 2.25... the counter-clockwise path from 157.2° to 270° is the short arc at 112.8°, so sweep should be 0. But I need to reconsider the SVG coordinate system—with y pointing down, sweep=1 actually traces clockwise on screen. Since my triangle outline (top-left → top-right → apex → back to top-left) goes clockwise visually, all corner arcs should use sweep=1. The left arc checks out: starting from roughly 9 o'clock and sweeping clockwise through 112° to 12 o'clock, so sweep=1 and large-arc=0. The right arc mirrors this—starting at 12 o'clock and rotating clockwise to about 3 o'clock, also with sweep=1. Both arcs are consistent with the original form.

Now I'm trying to round the coordinates to quarter units to simplify the numbers, but I'm running into a problem: when I adjust the arc endpoints to land on quarter values like 15.5 and 17.75, the resulting points no longer sit exactly on the radius 2.25 circle. A non-tangent arc would create a visible kink, so I need to pick the triangle dimensions more carefully so the geometry naturally aligns to quarter units. ward normal n = (cosφ, sinφ). So the arc endpoint E is at (15.5 + 2.25cosφ, 5.25 + 2.25 sinφ). The apex lies along the flank direction from E, and I need to solve for the angle φ such that the apex lands at x = 12 and y ≈ 19.6. Setting up the constraint equations: L sinφ = 3.5 + 2.25cosφ for the x-coordinate, and then solving for T using the y-coordinate with a test angle of 20°.

Testing φ = 20° gives T ≈ 21.45, which is too high. Trying φ = 23° yields T ≈ 19.26, and φ = 22.5° gives T ≈ 19.58, which is very close to the target of 19.6. So I'm settling on φ = 22.5° with the corresponding geometry parameters.

Now I'm calculating the bounding box for the nib path. The arc reaches its maximum x-coordinate of 17.75 at the 3 o'clock position, which falls within the arc's range, so the width spans from 6.25 to 17.75. The y-range goes from 3 to 19.58.

Writing SVG path... The tangent calculation gives me an apex at (12, 17.25), which makes the flank steeper than intended. Rather than chase exact tangency to two decimal places, I'll just stick with rounded values like the existing file uses — the visual impact matters more than perfect precision here. Testing different angles to find the right arc configuration—at φ = 25° the apex lands around 18.92, and φ = 24° gives 19.51, both still a bit long for the target positioning. Writing SVG path... Positioning the vent dot at y 8.5, I'm calculating the half-width of the nib at that height by tracing the flank slope, which gives me a half-width of 4.86 units. The dot with radius 1.3 leaves a gap of about 2.56 units from the flank, which checks out. The horizontal line sits at y 20.9 spanning from x 3 to x 21, creating a 1.4-unit gap below the apex.

With a 2-unit stroke, the apex's rounded join extends to about 20.5, overlapping slightly with the line's top edge at 19.9. Checking against the N1 render, the apex was at 19.6 and painted to 20.6, so there's overlap there too—and in the 48px version, the nib tip visibly merges with the line, which is the intended effect.

So I'm locking in: apex at (12, 19.5), line at y 20.9. The bounding box spans x 3–21 (width 18) and y 3–20.9 (height 17.9), centering at (12, 11.95). The keyline calculation gives a size of about 17.95, which is within the 8% tolerance. The body dimensions are 12 wide by 16.5 tall, and since the width doesn't meet the rounding threshold, the shape stays non-rounded.

Live area checks pass. Now I'll write this directly into the code and run the build to see the actual rendered result with keylines and measurements.
Settled on the nib standing on the line it writes. Let me commit the final geometry and run the real audit.

TypeScript is flagging that the function type in the Record is always defined, so my `| undefined` annotation doesn't actually widen the type the way I intended—the initializer still tells TS the value is always present. The real issue is that TS's function-truthiness check fires when it sees a function type, even if it's technically in a union with undefined, so the conditional at line 30 appears redundant to the type checker.

I can sidestep this by using the nullish coalescing operator to explicitly assign `null` when the lookup fails, then check against `null` instead of relying on truthiness—that way the type becomes `(() => JSX.Element) | null`, which is genuinely optional, and the conditional check becomes valid.

I see the issue now—TodoWrite has been removed from this Claude version, so tasks are created individually with `TaskCreate` returning an id, and updated separately with `TaskUpdate`. Since the board was designed to read an entire list in a single call that no longer exists, it's staying empty, which matches what the screenshot shows with those two "Updated tasks" rows containing just the task IDs and statuses.

The problem is that `TaskCreate` returns the id in its result, but `TaskUpdate` only has the id—there's no title to display. The `cli.ts` harness drops tool results for non-command tools, so I can't link them together that way. I could assume tasks are numbered sequentially by creation order (so the nth `TaskCreate` gets id "n"), which matches the observed "1" and "2", but that's fragile. The cleaner approach would be to preserve tool results for these task operations since they're small, or extract the id directly from the result. If the agent calls TaskList, we get the full list at once, but agents don't always do that. The cleaner approach is to maintain a task accumulator in the runner during a single run — when TaskCreate fires, I record the tool_use id and pending status; when the result comes back, I parse out the actual id and bind it; TaskUpdate applies changes to that tracked id. Then I emit the accumulated todos list at each step, which keeps the same shape the board already expects, so nothing downstream needs to change. The runner would need to hold this state per run in claude.ts rather than being pure per step, but that's fine since claude.ts already tracks runs. Though I'm realizing this approach is really Claude-specific since only Claude has these task tools — other providers have their own todo mechanisms.

+ import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest'
+ import { EAR_BLOCK } from '../src/renderer/src/media/voice/earWorklet'
+ import { FRAME, HEARD_RATE } from '../src/renderer/src/media/voice/gate'
+ import { ScribeTake } from '../src/renderer/src/media/scribe/take'
+ import { trim } from '../src/renderer/src/media/scribe/trim'
+ import { installFakeAudio } from './helpers/fake-audio'
+ 
+ // One dictation's worth of microphone, against a worklet that never really runs.
+ // What is driven here is the only thing that matters about it: the samples going
+ // in, the pieces coming out, and where each one says it began.
+ 
+ const RATE = 48_000
+ const BLOCKS_PER_SECOND = RATE / EAR_BLOCK
+ 
+ let ports: Array<{ onmessage: ((event: { data: Float32Array }) => void) | null }> = []
+ 
+ function installWorklet(): void {
+   ports = []
+   vi.stubGlobal(
+     'AudioWorkletNode',
+     class {
+       port = { onmessage: null, close: () => {} }
+       constructor() {
+         ports.push(this.port as never)
+       }
+       connect(): void {}
+       disconnect(): void {}
+     }
+   )
+   vi.stubGlobal(
+     'MediaStream',
+     class {
+       constructor(readonly tracks: unknown[]) {}
+     }
+   )
+   vi.stubGlobal('navigator', {
+     mediaDevices: {
+       getUserMedia: () =>
+         Promise.resolve({ getAudioTracks: () => [{ stop: () => {}, getSettings: () => ({}) }] })
+     }
+   })
+ }
+ 
+ // A block of what the microphone is hearing, at the rate the machine runs at.
+ const block = (level: number): Float32Array => {
+   const out = new Float32Array(EAR_BLOCK)
+   for (let i = 0; i < out.length; i++) out[i] = i % 2 === 0 ? level : -level
+   return out
+ }
+ 
+ const feed = (seconds: number, level: number): void => {
+   const blocks = Math.round(seconds * BLOCKS_PER_SECOND)
+   for (let i = 0; i < blocks; i++) ports[0]?.onmessage?.({ data: block(level) })
+ }
+ 
+ describe('the microphone a dictation is taken through', () => {
+   beforeEach(() => {
+     installFakeAudio()
+     installWorklet()
+   })
+ 
+   afterEach(() => vi.unstubAllGlobals())
+ 
+   it('keeps every sample from the moment it was told to', async () => {
+     const take = new ScribeTake({ onPiece: () => {} })
+     expect(await take.start()).toBe(null)
+     take.record(true)
+     feed(1, 0.2)
+     expect(take.rest().audio.length).toBeGreaterThan(HEARD_RATE * 0.9)
+     take.close()
+   })
+ 
+   // A microphone that is standing open is not a microphone anything is being
+   // heard through, which is the whole of what makes keeping it open bearable.
+   it('keeps nothing at all while it is only open', async () => {
+     const take = new ScribeTake({ onPiece: () => {} })
+     await take.start()
+     feed(2, 0.2)
+     expect(take.rest().audio.length).toBe(0)
+     take.record(true)
+     feed(1, 0.2)
+     expect(take.rest().audio.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)
+     take.close()
+   })
+ 
+   it('hands a finished stretch over while somebody is still talking', async () => {
+     const pieces: Array<{ seconds: number; at: number }> = []
+     const take = new ScribeTake({
+       onPiece: (audio, at) => pieces.push({ seconds: audio.length / HEARD_RATE, at })
+     })
+     await take.start()
+     take.record(true)
+     feed(4, 0.25)
+     expect(pieces).toHaveLength(0)
+     // The pause after it is what says the stretch is finished with.
+     feed(1.2, 0.001)
+     expect(pieces).toHaveLength(1)
+     expect(pieces[0].at).toBe(0)
+     expect(pieces[0].seconds).toBeGreaterThan(4)
+     take.close()
+   })
+ 
+   it('starts the next stretch where the last one ended', async () => {
+     const pieces: Array<{ seconds: number; at: number }> = []
+     const take = new ScribeTake({
+       onPiece: (audio, at) => pieces.push({ seconds: audio.length / HEARD_RATE, at })
+     })
+     await take.start()
+     take.record(true)
+     feed(4, 0.25)
+     feed(1.2, 0.001)
+     feed(4, 0.25)
+     feed(1.2, 0.001)
+     expect(pieces).toHaveLength(2)
+     expect(pieces[1].at).toBeCloseTo(pieces[0].seconds, 1)
+     const rest = take.rest()
+     expect(rest.at).toBeCloseTo(pieces[1].at + pieces[1].seconds, 1)
+     take.close()
+   })
+ 
+   // A pause inside a sentence is not the end of one, and a run too short to be
+   // worth reading on its own stays with what follows it.
+   it('does not break on a gap too short to have finished anything', async () => {
+     const pieces: number[] = []
+     const take = new ScribeTake({ onPiece: (_audio, at) => pieces.push(at) })
+     await take.start()
+     take.record(true)
+     feed(1, 0.25)
+     feed(1.2, 0.001)
+     feed(1, 0.25)
+     expect(pieces).toHaveLength(0)
+     take.close()
+   })
+ 
+   it('leaves nothing behind when it closes', async () => {
+     const take = new ScribeTake({ onPiece: () => {} })
+     await take.start()
+     take.record(true)
+     feed(2, 0.25)
+     take.close()
+     expect(take.listening).toBe(false)
+     expect(take.rest().audio.length).toBe(0)
+   })
+ })
+ 
+ const quiet = (frames: number): number[] => new Array(frames * FRAME).fill(0.0004)
+ 
+ const loud = (frames: number): number[] =>
+   Array.from({ length: frames * FRAME }, (_, i) => (i % 2 === 0 ? 0.3 : -0.3))
+ 
+ describe('the quiet at both ends of a dictation', () => {
+   it('takes the room off the front and the back', () => {
+     const audio = new Float32Array([...quiet(30), ...loud(40), ...quiet(30)])
+     const { audio: cut, spoke } = trim(audio, HEARD_RATE)
+     expect(spoke).toBe(true)
+     expect(cut.length).toBeLessThan(audio.length)
+     expect(cut.length).toBeGreaterThan(40 * FRAME)
+   })
+ 
+   // Speech starts before it is loud enough to measure, so a word missing its
+   // first consonant is one whisper then invents.
+   it('leaves room in front of the first word', () => {
+     const audio = new Float32Array([...quiet(30), ...loud(40), ...quiet(30)])
+     const kept = trim(audio, HEARD_RATE).audio.length
+     expect(kept).toBeGreaterThan(40 * FRAME + FRAME * 4)
+   })
+ 
+   it('says a room where nobody spoke said nothing', () => {
+     const { audio, spoke } = trim(new Float32Array(quiet(80)), HEARD_RATE)
+     expect(spoke).toBe(false)
+     expect(audio.length).toBe(0)
+   })
+ 
+   it('leaves something too short to measure exactly as it is', () => {
+     const audio = new Float32Array(loud(1))

step.text:
Jamel's pointing out that instead of building a Claude-specific fix, the solution should live in Crew itself so it works across any model. Rather than parsing each CLI's own todo tool, Crew should manage the board directly—giving every agent its own ticket tools over HTTP, using the same pattern as `/agents/spawn` in the preamble, which is exactly how the helpers already work.

So the board lives at `/tickets/*` on the host's HTTP, and agents create, move, and review tickets through curl calls. Crew owns the board entirely, which means no more parsing prose for fenced cards, no per-provider parsers that break when Anthropic renames a tool, and the empty board at the root stops depending on whatever list a CLI happens to expose. I could keep `stepTodos` as a fallback for non-tickets threads since it costs nothing, but the real board is Crew's own. Now I need to think carefully about the scope and design—what's the right way to build this.

The key insight is that ticket calls should land as events on the thread itself, so the host writes one step per call and `boardOf` still reconstructs the board from the thread's steps. This keeps replay free and doesn't add anything new to the sync loop beyond what a step already costs. The only change is the input source: Crew's HTTP endpoint instead of whatever tool the CLI exposes. It's the same pattern as helpers—`/agents/spawn` returns an ID immediately, and the record is the chip.

So the cleanest move is to add Crew's own ticket API in the preamble as a short block like the helpers section, with curl examples for every provider. The host turns each call into a card on the thread, and `boardOf` folds the board off those cards the same way it does now. This means dropping the fenced `work` blocks entirely since they were the "cards written beside prose" design, and with a real API those blocks become redundant.

I should also drop the dependency on `stepTodos` for the columns in tickets mode—keep it as a fallback for threads without tickets, but let Crew own the board when tickets are active.

For this turn, I need to deliver the host HTTP routes, an event shape for ticket moves, the preamble text, update `boardOf` to read the new records, and write tests. But I need to be careful about file boundaries since two agents editing the same files can't merge cleanly. Let me first confirm the current wiring before I commit to the split. Gathering the codebase now.

All the test suites are passing, so now I'm drafting the AGENTS.md rule about selectability. I'm keeping the tone consistent with the project—straightforward and direct, without flourishes. The rule explains how the base stylesheet removes text selection from the body, then restores it only for interactive elements like fields and textareas, while buttons, tabs, labels, and headings remain non-selectable to emphasize they're meant to be interacted with rather than highlighted.

For content boxes—things users write, agent responses, diffs, and command output—I'm adding `select-text` back so people can copy them. Markers inside those boxes like diff symbols and command prompts get `select-none` so only the actual code gets copied. I'm also noting that closing interactions check whether text is being selected first, so a drag-to-copy action doesn't get interrupted.

This is a longer bullet point, but that matches the style of other rules in this file. I'm placing it before the `--color-selection` line since it makes sense to cover the default behavior first, then the visual band that shows what's selected.

files.diff:
- - The selection band is written down once, as `--color-selection`, and `::selection` reads it.
+ - Nothing in the app is selectable until it says it is. The app is a window rather than a page, so the base layer in `styles.css` takes `user-select` off the body, and a field, a textarea and anything editable get it back at once. A button, a tab, a label, a heading and the line under an empty screen are things to press and read, and a drag that started anywhere near one used to paint half the chrome blue. Content asks for it back with `select-text` on the box that holds it, and only there: what somebody wrote, what an agent said, a plan, a diff, a command and what it printed. The rule stands in the base layer and nowhere else, because a plain rule in that file beats every utility whichever order the two are written in, and a default nothing can turn off is worse than no default at all. A marker standing inside one of those boxes wears `select-none` of its own, the `+` and `−` down a diff and the `$` in front of a command, so what comes away is the code and not the gutter. A click that closes what it is written over, the way a thought folds up, asks `selecting()` first, or a drag to copy the words takes them off the screen as it lets go. `tests/selection-rule.test.ts` holds the default and `tests/selection-probe.test.ts` holds the pair, a name shut and a message open.
+ - The selection band is written down once, as `--color-selection`, and `::selection` reads it.

step.text:
Events with `ticket.*` namespacing and thread-scoped replay seem like the right approach—they're naturally broadcast and `boardOf` can fold them together. But I'm running into tension with my earlier principle that nothing about a board gets persisted; an event for every ticket movement across a run with multiple tickets could overwhelm the sync loop.

Actually, that concern doesn't hold up. A typical run generates maybe 30 events total—creates, moves, decisions—which is negligible compared to the dozens or hundreds of steps already logged for tool calls. The real win is that events become Crew's own record of what happened, not a re-reading of some external tool's state, which is what matters for steering.

So I'm committing to `ticket.*` events. The refactor is substantial—shared types, host routes, session methods, event definitions, renderer, tests—but I can parallelize the work by splitting files strategically.

I'll spawn a helper now to handle the runner fallback, write the core types and events myself, then spawn another helper for the server routes once the interface is solid, handle the renderer myself, and finish with tests. I need to understand the task result shape and how it flows through the system—TaskCreate takes a subject and description, TaskUpdate uses taskId and status, and results come back as activities with matching IDs but empty names. Since shell tools are the only ones that persist output, I'll route task results through without storing them as step output. Let me write the helper task and clean up the probe afterward.

In the crew repo (Electron + TypeScript, run yarn tsc --noEmit to typecheck), fix the fallback that reads an agent CLI's own task list, which broke because Claude Code replaced its whole-list tool with per-task ones.

BACKGROUND. src/runner/providers/detail.ts exports stepTodos(input): StepTodo[] | undefined. StepTodo is {text: string, status: 0todo0 | 0doing0 | 0done0} in src/shared/llm.ts (quotes shown as zeros here, use real quotes). It is called from claude.ts, kimi.ts, grok.ts, codex.ts at the tool_use block, and whatever it returns rides on the step as step.todos. Its internal todoList() looks for an array under the keys todos / plan / items / steps in the tool input. That works for TodoWrite, update_plan and Codex todo_list.

THE BREAK. Current Claude Code no longer has TodoWrite. It has TaskCreate, TaskUpdate, TaskList, TaskGet. None of them ever carries the whole list in the tool input:
  TaskCreate input: {"subject":"Draw the rows","description":"...","activeForm":"Drawing the rows"}  (activeForm optional)
  TaskCreate tool result text, verified empirically: `Task #1 created successfully: Draw the rows`
  TaskUpdate input: {"taskId":"1","status":"completed"}  and it can also carry subject, description, activeForm, owner
  TaskUpdate status values: pending | in_progress | completed | deleted
  TaskList input: {} and its result is a summary of every task
So stepTodos returns undefined for all of these and the step carries no list at all.

WHAT TO BUILD. A small accumulator so that a step for one of these per-task tools still carries the WHOLE list as step.todos, folded from every such call so far in the run. Ids are ordinal strings ("1", "2"). Bind the id from the TaskCreate tool result, since the input has no id: cli.ts already receives the result as a second activity carrying the same activity id as the tool_use, at src/runner/providers/cli.ts around line 269-285, where a toolNames Map<string,string> from activity id to tool name already exists (note it drops output unless isShellTool, so read the result text before that drop rather than changing what is stored on the step). Parse the number out of the result forgivingly (`Task #(\d+)`), and fall back to creation order if the result cannot be parsed, so a create with an unreadable result still lands.

RULES. Status deleted removes the task from the list. Keep the existing whole-list path working exactly as it does now, all four providers, all the existing spellings in DOING and DONE and Codex booleans: this is an addition, not a rewrite. Keep the ordinal ids out of StepTodo, which stays {text, status}. Order the list the way the tasks were created. Reuse the TODO_LIMIT and TODO_TEXT_LIMIT already in detail.ts. Prefer subject for the ticket text; activeForm is only used by the separate todoDetail() narration and you must not change which one that prefers.

SCOPE. Only src/runner/providers/*.ts, plus ONE new test file tests/step-todos.test.ts. Do not touch src/shared/tickets.ts, src/server/**, src/renderer/**, tests/tickets.test.ts, AGENTS.md: another agent is editing those right now and two agents in one file is the one thing that cannot merge.

Fix one rule in src/shared/scribeTidy.ts and extend tests/scribe-tidy.test.ts to cover it. Touch NO other file. Read AGENTS.md first and follow it (no em dashes, no code comments except where a rule needs explaining in the project voice, TypeScript, small files).

Context: scribeTidy.ts turns whisper output into written text for a dictation feature. It already works and has about 50 passing tests in tests/scribe-tidy.test.ts. Do not regress any of them. Its self-correction rule currently cuts back to the start of the CURRENT sentence. Two real gaps were found by running real speech through the real model:

GAP 1, the important one. When a correction phrase OPENS a sentence, so there is nothing before it in the current sentence to delete, it must reach back and take the WHOLE previous sentence with it. People dictate in sentences, and whisper punctuates them, so this is the common shape, not an edge case.

  Broken now:
    [{"Let's use redis.",0,1.5},{"Scratch that.",2.4,3.0},{"Let's use postgres.",3.4,4.6}]
    gives  "Let's use redis. Let's use postgres."
    must give  "Let's use postgres."

  Already right, keep it right:
    [{"let's use redis,",0,1.5},{"scratch that,",1.6,2.0},{"let's use postgres",2.1,3.2}]
    gives  "Let's use postgres."

  Only one sentence back, never two. "A. B. Scratch that. C." leaves "A. C." A second correction straight after the first may take another one, since that is a person correcting twice.

GAP 2, smaller. Add these to the correction phrases, all of which mean the same thing when they stand as their own clause or sentence: "actually wait", "actually hold on", "hold on", "sorry no", "no sorry", "scratch all of that". Keep the existing conservatism: they must only fire at a boundary, so "hold on to the branch" and "we should hold on until Friday" must survive untouched. If you judge any one of these too risky to include, leave it out and say which and why.

Also confirm this real case now works, and add it as a test: [{"I think we should ship it today.",0,2.0},{"Actually, wait.",2.6,3.2},{"I think we should ship it tomorrow.",3.6,5.6}] must give "I think we should ship it tomorrow."

Add tests for every case above plus: a correction opening the very first sentence with nothing before it (must not throw, must just drop itself), "scratch all that" still taking the whole dictation, and a couple of longer realistic dictations where a mid-dictation correction reaches back one sentence and the sentences either side of it are untouched.

+ // A correction is a clause of its own, marked off at both ends, which is what
+ // leaves "hold on to the branch" as somebody holding on to a branch. Standing at
+ // the head of a sentence it has nothing in front of it to take, so it reaches
+ // back for the sentence before it, which is how people dictate: one sentence,
+ // then the one that replaces it. Only ever one back, and a second correction
+ // straight after takes another, since that is somebody correcting twice.
+ const corrected = (words: Word[]): Word[] => {
+   const out: Word[] = []
+   const starts = [0]
+   for (let index = 0; index < words.length; ) {
+     const cut = opens(words, index)
+       ? CUTS.find(entry => matches(words, index, entry.phrase) && closes(words, index + entry.phrase.length))
+       : undefined
+     if (!cut) {
+       const word = words[index]
+       out.push(word)
+       if (ends(word) || (words[index + 1]?.gap ?? 0) >= SENTENCE_GAP) starts.push(out.length)
+       index += 1
+       continue
+     }
+     if (!cut.whole && starts.length > 1 && starts[starts.length - 1] === out.length) starts.pop()
+     if (cut.whole) starts.length = 1
+     const from = cut.whole ? 0 : starts[starts.length - 1]
+     const gap = out[from]?.gap ?? words[index].gap
+     out.length = from
+     const next = words[index + cut.phrase.length]
+     if (next) next.gap = Math.max(next.gap, gap)
+     index += cut.phrase.length
+   }
+   return out
+ }

+ import type { StepTodo } from '../../shared/llm'
+ import { stepTodos } from './detail'
+ import type { ParsedActivity, TaskCall } from './types'
+ 
+ // Claude Code has no whole-list tool any more. A task is made, changed and read
+ // one call at a time, so nothing a CLI hands over carries the list, and these
+ // are the four calls it is written with, however a CLI spells them.
+ const TASK_TOOLS = new Set(['taskcreate', 'taskupdate', 'tasklist', 'taskget'])
+ 
+ const toolKey = (name: string): string => name.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z]/g, '')
+ 
+ const isTaskTool = (name: string): boolean => TASK_TOOLS.has(toolKey(name))
+ 
+ const str = (value: unknown): string => (typeof value === 'string' ? value.trim() : '')
+ 
+ const idOf = (record: Record<string, unknown>): string => {
+   const raw = record['taskId'] ?? record['task_id'] ?? record['id']
+   return typeof raw === 'number' ? String(raw) : str(raw)
+ }
+ 
+ export function taskCall(name: string, input: unknown): TaskCall | undefined {
+   const tool = toolKey(name)
+   if (!TASK_TOOLS.has(tool)) return undefined
+   const record = input && typeof input === 'object' ? (input as Record<string, unknown>) : {}
+   return {
+     kind: tool === 'taskcreate' ? 'create' : tool === 'taskupdate' ? 'change' : 'read',
+     id: idOf(record),
+     subject: str(record['subject']),
+     description: str(record['description']),
+     status: str(record['status']).toLowerCase()
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ interface Task {
+   id: string
+   subject: string
+   description: string
+   status: string
+ }
+ 
+ export interface TaskLedger {
+   todos(name: string, activity: ParsedActivity): StepTodo[] | undefined
+ }
+ 
+ // A create says no id at all, and the only place one is ever said is the line
+ // the tool hands back, so it is read out of that as loosely as it can be.
+ const NAMED = /task\s*#(\d+)/i
+ 
+ // The list itself, folded from those single calls, so a step for one of them
+ // still says what the whole of the work is. It belongs to the run rather than
+ // to the module: two agents on one machine are two lists.
+ export function taskLedger(): TaskLedger {
+   const tasks: Task[] = []
+   const made = new Map<string, Task>()
+   let created = 0
+ 
+   const add = (id: string, call: TaskCall): Task => {
+     const task = { id, subject: call.subject, description: call.description, status: call.status || 'pending' }
+     tasks.push(task)
+     return task
+   }
+ 
+   const create = (activityId: string, call: TaskCall): void => {
+     // A CLI can report the same call more than once, and a task made twice is a
+     // row that never goes away. Until the result names it, a task answers to
+     // the order it was made in, which is what the numbering follows anyway.
+     if (made.has(activityId)) return
+     made.set(activityId, add(String(++created), call))
+   }
+ 
+   const change = (call: TaskCall): void => {
+     if (!call.id) return
+     const task = tasks.find(entry => entry.id === call.id)
+     if (call.status === 'deleted') {
+       if (task) tasks.splice(tasks.indexOf(task), 1)
+       return
+     }
+     // A list can outlive the run that wrote it, so a change naming a task this
+     // has never seen is taken as the task rather than dropped.
+     if (!task) {
+       if (call.subject || call.description) add(call.id, call)
+       return
+     }
+     if (call.subject) task.subject = call.subject
+     if (call.description) task.description = call.description
+     if (call.status) task.status = call.status
+   }
+ 
+   const bind = (activityId: string, output: string): void => {
+     const task = made.get(activityId)
+     const found = NAMED.exec(output)
+     if (task && found) task.id = found[1]
+   }
+ 
+   return {
+     todos(name, activity) {
+       if (!isTaskTool(name)) return undefined
+       if (activity.status === 'finished') bind(activity.id, activity.output ?? '')
+       else if (activity.task?.kind === 'create') create(activity.id, activity.task)
+       else if (activity.task?.kind === 'change') change(activity.task)
+       // Read back out through the whole-list path, so a list folded from single
+       // calls lands on the same limits and the same words for a state.
+       return stepTodos({
+         todos: tasks.map(task => ({ content: task.subject, description: task.description, status: task.status }))
+       })
+     }
+   }
+ }
